title: Follow That Dream (with poem: Believe in Yourself)

topics.title: Ambition: dreams, goals and talking about the future

learn.hook: Every big dream starts as a tiny 'what if'. What if you are the next great scientist, singer or athlete?
points: The lesson 'Follow That Dream' is about ambition: having a goal and working steadily towards it.

Key words: ambition (a strong wish to achieve something), aspire (to hope and work to achieve something), goal, obstacle (something in the way), persevere (keep going despite difficulty), milestone (an important stage of progress).
Talking about the future: 'will' for predictions and on-the-spot decisions; 'be going to' for plans and for things we can see coming ('Look at those clouds; it is going to rain').
The present continuous can show fixed arrangements ('I am meeting my coach tomorrow'); the simple present is used for timetables ('The train leaves at 6:10').
Big dreams become real through small, steady steps.

example.q: Choose the right future form: 'Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.'
steps: We can see evidence now: dark clouds.
When present evidence shows something is about to happen, we use 'be going to'.

learn.reallife: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam grew up in Rameswaram and sold newspapers as a boy before becoming a scientist and President of India. Kalpana Chawla became the first woman of Indian origin to go to space.

games.title: Dream words
pairs: A strong wish to achieve something
Hope and work to achieve a goal

items.text: Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.
The Vande Bharat train ___ at 6:10 every morning.
I ___ my coach at 5 p.m. tomorrow; we have fixed the time.
Perhaps one day robots ___ cook all our meals.

quiz.q: What does 'aspire' mean?
options: To hope and work to achieve something
quiz.explain: To aspire is to have a strong hope and to work towards it.
steps: 'Aspire' = to hope and work to achieve something.
Answer: To hope and work to achieve something
quiz.mistake: Links the word only with breathing

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'obstacle'?
quiz.explain: An obstacle is something in your way, like a hurdle.
steps: An obstacle is something in the way.
A hurdle means the same.
Answer: Hurdle
quiz.mistake: Picks something helpful instead of something that blocks

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'Watch out! That glass ___ fall off the edge.'
quiz.explain: We can see the glass about to fall, so we use 'is going to'.
steps: We can see the glass about to fall.
For things we can see coming, use 'be going to'.
Answer: is going to
quiz.mistake: Uses a past form for something that has not yet happened

quiz.q: Choose the correct form: 'According to the timetable, the exam ___ at 10 a.m. on Monday.'
quiz.explain: The simple present is used for timetables and schedules.
steps: Timetables and schedules use the simple present.
Subject 'the exam' is singular: starts.
Answer: starts
quiz.mistake: Thinks the simple present cannot talk about the future

quiz.q: Read: 'At twelve, Neha dreamt of mountaineering, but she got breathless on the school stairs. She began with a walk around her colony each morning, then jogging, then weekend treks near Pune. Three years later, she reached a Himalayan base camp.' What does this show?
options: Big goals can be reached through small, steady steps
quiz.explain: Neha moved from walks to jogs to treks, step by step, until she reached her goal.
steps: Neha went from walks to jogging to treks, step by step.
Three years later she reached a base camp.
Answer: Big goals can be reached through small, steady steps
quiz.mistake: Misses the step-by-step progress in the passage

quiz.q: What was Kalpana Chawla's famous achievement?
options: First woman of Indian origin to go to space
First Indian to win an Olympic medal
quiz.explain: Kalpana Chawla flew on the Space Shuttle and was the first woman of Indian origin in space.
steps: Kalpana Chawla flew on the Space Shuttle.
She was the first woman of Indian origin in space.
Answer: First woman of Indian origin to go to space
quiz.mistake: Mixes her up with other Indian 'firsts'

quiz.q: What is the noun form of 'ambitious'?
quiz.explain: 'Ambition' is the noun; 'ambitious' is the adjective.
steps: 'Ambitious' is the adjective.
The noun is 'ambition'.
Answer: Ambition
quiz.mistake: Picks an adverb or a made-up form

quiz.q: 'Passing the Grade 5 music exam was a milestone for Ishita.' What does 'milestone' mean here?
quiz.explain: Here 'milestone' is used figuratively for an important step forward.
steps: 'Milestone' is used figuratively here.
It means an important stage of progress.
Answer: An important stage of progress
quiz.mistake: Takes the word in its literal roadside meaning

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: "I dream of flying over the Himalayas, but I can only fly to the next tree! What should I do?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Set a goal, take small steps and keep going. Tree today, Himalayas one day!
teach.nudge: Hmm, should I try the Himalayas tomorrow? Or is there a better way to reach a big goal?

revise.summary: 'Follow That Dream' is about ambition: having a goal and working steadily towards it. The topic builds words like aspire, obstacle, persevere and milestone, and ways of talking about the future.
focus: Present continuous for arrangements; simple present for timetables
remember: ambition (noun), ambitious (adjective); aspire; obstacle = hurdle; milestone = important stage
be going to = plan or something we can see coming
traps: Use 'is going to' for things you can see about to happen.
Don't use 'start' with a singular subject in a timetable: 'the exam starts'.

learn.hook: What do you say to yourself just before an exam? Those quiet words might be the most important ones of the day!
points: Self-belief is confidence in your own abilities. Self-doubt is its opposite. An optimistic person expects good things; a pessimistic person expects the worst.
Idioms: 'keep your chin up' (stay cheerful in hard times), 'rise to the occasion' (do well when it really matters), 'never say die' (never give up), 'against all odds' (despite great difficulties).
Positive self-talk turns 'I can't do this' into 'I can't do this yet, but I'm learning.'

Contrast words: 'although' and 'even though' are followed by a clause (Although she was nervous, she sang). 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or an -ing form (Despite her nerves, she sang). We never say 'despite of'.

example.q: Join the two sentences using 'although': 'She was nervous. She sang beautifully.'
steps: 'Although' introduces the contrasting idea, which has a subject and a verb: she was nervous.
Add a comma, then the main clause.
example.answer: Although she was nervous, she sang beautifully.

learn.reallife: Before a match, a speech or a board exam, many people take a deep breath and remind themselves how much they have prepared.

games.title: Although or despite?
items: ___ it was raining, the match continued.
___ he felt tired, he finished the race.
___ she was afraid of heights, she climbed the wall.
___ the hall was noisy, we heard the speech.
___ the rain, the match continued.
___ feeling tired, he finished the race.
___ her fear of heights, she climbed the wall.
___ the noise, we heard the speech.

games.title: Self-belief and grammar
items: 'Despite of the rain' is correct English.
We say 'despite the rain' or 'in spite of the rain', never 'despite of'.
'Although' is followed by a clause with a subject and a verb.
For example: Although it was late, we kept working.
'Keep your chin up' means stay cheerful in a difficult time.
It encourages someone not to lose hope.
Self-doubt is the opposite of self-belief.
Self-doubt means lacking confidence in yourself.
'Never say die' means give up early.
It means never give up.
An optimistic person expects good things to happen.
Optimism is a hopeful outlook.

quiz.q: What is 'self-belief'?
quiz.explain: Self-belief means trusting that you can do something.
steps: Self-belief = confidence in your own abilities.
Answer: Confidence in your own abilities
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'self-belief' with being selfish

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'optimistic'?
quiz.explain: A pessimistic person expects bad outcomes, the opposite of optimistic.
steps: Optimistic expects good; pessimistic expects the worst.
Answer: Pessimistic
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly joins 'He was tired' and 'He kept practising' using 'although'?
options: Although he was tired, but he kept practising.
Although tired he was, he kept practising.
Although he was tired, he kept practising.
He was although tired, he kept practising.
quiz.explain: 'Although' starts the first clause; we do not add 'but' as well.
steps: 'Although' introduces the first clause.
Don't add 'but' as well.
Answer: Although he was tired, he kept practising.
quiz.mistake: Uses both 'although' and 'but' in one sentence

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Despite of her injury, she played.
Despite she was injured, she played.
Despite to her injury, she played.
quiz.explain: 'Despite' is followed directly by a noun phrase: despite her injury.
steps: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form; never 'despite of'.
Answer: Despite her injury, she played.
quiz.mistake: Adds 'of' after 'despite' or uses a full clause after it

quiz.q: 'When the team needed one last goal, Arjun rose to the occasion.' What does this mean?
options: He stood up from his seat
He did well when it really mattered
quiz.explain: To rise to the occasion is to perform well at an important moment.
steps: 'Rise to the occasion' = do well when it really matters.
Answer: He did well when it really mattered
quiz.mistake: Takes 'rose' literally

quiz.q: 'Against all odds, the village team won the state title.' What does 'against all odds' mean?
quiz.explain: 'Against all odds' means succeeding even though success seemed very unlikely.
steps: 'Against all odds' = despite very great difficulties.
Answer: Despite very great difficulties
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'odds' means something unfair

quiz.q: Which is a positive self-talk version of 'I can't solve this'?
options: I can't solve this yet, but I'll keep trying.
quiz.explain: Adding 'yet' and a plan to keep trying shows belief that you can improve.
steps: Positive self-talk adds 'yet' and a plan to keep going.
Answer: I can't solve this yet, but I'll keep trying.
quiz.mistake: Thinks being honest means being negative about yourself

quiz.q: Read: 'Before the debate, Ira's hands were cold and her voice shook. She told herself, "I have practised; I am ready." She stepped up, took a deep breath and spoke clearly.' What helped Ira?
quiz.explain: Her positive self-talk about her practice gave her the confidence to speak.
steps: Ira told herself 'I have practised; I am ready.'
Reminding herself of her preparation gave her confidence.
Answer: Reminding herself of her preparation
quiz.mistake: Picks an event the passage does not describe

teach.ask: Gappu trembles: "My first flying test is tomorrow and I keep thinking 'I can't!' How do I believe in myself?"
teach.praise: Chirp! I have practised, so I'll tell myself 'I can do this'. Not 'I can't', just 'not yet'!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what could I say to myself instead of 'I can't'? And what have I already done to get ready?

revise.summary: Self-belief is confidence in your own abilities. The topic covers optimistic vs pessimistic, idioms of courage, positive self-talk, and contrast words although/even though and despite/in spite of.
remember: keep your chin up, rise to the occasion, never say die, against all odds
Despite/in spite of + noun or -ing (never 'despite of')
traps: Don't write 'despite of' or 'despite she was'.

topics.title: Believe in Yourself: imperatives, sentence types and diary writing

learn.hook: 'Stand up! Try again! Believe!' Notice anything? Poems of courage love command words!
points: The poem 'Believe in Yourself' in this lesson encourages the reader to trust their own strength and keep going.
Imperative sentences give commands, advice or encouragement. They start with the base form of a verb, and the subject 'you' is understood: 'Stand firm.'
The four types of sentences are declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request) and exclamatory (strong feeling, often with What or How and an exclamation mark).
Repeating a word at the start of lines (anaphora) and making storms or doubts speak (personification) add force to a poem.
A diary entry has the date, day and time, is written in the first person, records events and feelings in an informal style, and ends with your name.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'Believe the seed that dreams of tree,
Believe the stream that seeks the sea;
When storms say "Stop!" and doubts say "No,"
Stand up, stand firm, and still say "Go!"
The sky is not your ceiling, friend:
It's just the start, it's not the end.'
Find an imperative and explain 'The sky is not your ceiling'.
steps: 'Stand up, stand firm' begins with base verbs and gives encouragement: imperative.
A ceiling stops you from going higher; the poet says the sky is not such a limit.
So the line means there is no fixed limit to how far you can rise.
example.answer: Imperative: 'Stand up, stand firm'. 'The sky is not your ceiling' means there is no limit to what you can achieve.

learn.reallife: Keeping a diary of your goals and small wins, like finishing a chapter or a tough practice session, is a great way to build self-belief.

games.title: What type of sentence?
items: Close the window, please.
Never give up.
Believe in yourself.
Will you join the race?
Why are you smiling?
Have you finished your practice?
What a beautiful song!
How tall the mountain is!
What a lovely surprise!

games.title: Write a diary entry
games.prompt: Put the parts of a diary entry in order
items: Date, day and time
Dear Diary
What happened today, in the first person
How you felt about it
Your name

quiz.q: 'Believe the seed that dreams of tree, / Believe the stream that seeks the sea.' Which device does the repeated 'Believe' at the start of lines show?
quiz.explain: Repeating the same word at the beginning of lines is anaphora.
steps: Repeating a word at the start of lines is anaphora.
Answer: Anaphora
quiz.mistake: Confuses repetition at the start of lines with sound devices

quiz.q: What does 'The sky is not your ceiling' mean?
options: There is no limit to what you can achieve
You should never look at the sky
quiz.explain: A ceiling is an upper limit; the line says even the sky does not limit you.
steps: A ceiling is an upper limit.
The line says even the sky does not limit you.
Answer: There is no limit to what you can achieve
quiz.mistake: Reads the metaphor literally

quiz.q: 'When storms say "Stop!" and doubts say "No"'. Storms and doubts speaking is an example of:
quiz.explain: Speaking is a human action given to storms and doubts.
steps: Storms and doubts cannot really speak.
Giving them a human action is personification.
Answer: Personification
quiz.mistake: Does not see that non-human things are acting like people

quiz.q: Which of these is an imperative sentence?
quiz.explain: It begins with a base verb and gives encouragement, with 'you' understood.
steps: Imperatives start with a base verb; 'you' is understood.
'Stand up and try again.' does this.
Answer: Stand up and try again.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up imperative with declarative or exclamatory sentences

quiz.q: What is the subject of an imperative sentence like 'Stand firm'?
quiz.explain: In imperatives the subject 'you' is understood, not written.
steps: In imperatives the subject is not written.
It is the understood 'you'.
Answer: The understood 'you'
quiz.mistake: Thinks a command has no subject at all

quiz.q: In which person is a diary entry usually written?
quiz.explain: A diary records your own experiences, so it uses 'I'.
steps: A diary records your own events and feelings.
So it is written in the first person (I).
Answer: First person (I)
quiz.mistake: Writes about yourself as 'he' or 'she'

quiz.q: What is the central idea of the original poem 'Believe the seed that dreams of tree...'?
options: Trust yourself and keep going despite doubts
quiz.explain: The poem urges us to believe, stand firm and go on, because there is no limit.
steps: The poem urges us to believe, stand firm and go on despite storms and doubts.
Answer: Trust yourself and keep going despite doubts
quiz.mistake: Picks a literal detail instead of the message

quiz.q: Which sentence is exclamatory?
options: What a brave climber she is!
quiz.explain: It expresses strong feeling with 'What' and an exclamation mark.
steps: Exclamatory sentences show strong feeling, often with What/How and '!'.
Answer: What a brave climber she is!
quiz.mistake: Mixes up exclamatory and imperative sentences

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How does a poem make me feel brave? And what is an imperative?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Imperatives like 'Stand up!' and repeating 'Believe' make the poem cheer me on. I believe in myself!
teach.nudge: But what kind of sentences does the poem use to encourage me, and what does it want me to believe?

revise.summary: 'Believe in Yourself' encourages trusting your strength and going on. The topic covers imperative sentences, the four sentence types, anaphora and personification, and diary-entry format.
remember: 'The sky is not your ceiling' = no limit to what you can achieve
Diary: date, day, time; first person; informal; ends with your name
traps: Don't think an imperative has no subject; its subject is the understood 'you'.
A diary is written in the first person, not the third.
